rows.label: Consumption per person of refugees after resettlement in a rich country, as a share of the US survey average
rows.explainer: Refugees who reach the US, Canada, Germany or Australia start poor and catch up slowly: we take their consumption per person over the years counted at the spending of the lowest-income fifth of US households against the average (@united_states.ce_lowest_quintile_vs_all_2024, 0.45 per household; per person it is higher, but refugee households are large), from 0.3 (the first years, on reception benefits; destinations in Europe, a little poorer than the US) to 0.7 (the second fifth's 0.64, @united_states.ce_second_quintile_vs_all_2024, as refugees' employment catches up with the native-born within about a decade). Read by both IRAP models.

rows.label: Consumption per person a day of refugees waiting outside the Americas for a pathway (2021 PPP dollars)
rows.explainer: Refugees waiting in Jordan and Lebanon (Syrian, Iraqi, Sudanese and Yemeni refugees), in East Africa (Congolese, Somali and Eritrean refugees in Kenya) and in Afghanistan and Pakistan. Anchors: Kenya's survey mean of 4.44 a day (@survey_consumption.ken_survey_mean_2021ppp_day), above what camp refugees consume; most Syrian refugees in Lebanon live below the survival expenditure basket; Afghans' incomes collapsed after 2021. Our judgment is 4, from 3 to 7. Read by both IRAP models (the legal-services model blends it with Central American families' consumption).

rows.label: How long a resettled refugee's higher consumption lasts (years)
rows.explainer: Resettled refugees (IRAP's clients, the refugees HIAS resettles) are mostly young adults and their children, and rarely return. The gain lasts the rest of their lives, about 40 years for an adult of 35, less any later return; we count 30 years, from 15 (adults near 50, some returns) to 45 (children). Whether they would have moved later anyway is not here but in each model's counterfactual. Discounted at the shared rate where it is read. Read by the IRAP and HIAS resettlement models.

rows.label: Death rate of resettled refugees in a rich country at the clients' ages (deaths per person-year)
rows.explainer: US deaths at ages 15 to 49 run at about 1.5 to 2 per 1,000 a year, children's far lower and older adults' higher; with IRAP's clients mostly working-age adults and their children, 0.002, from 0.0012 to 0.003. Read by both IRAP models as the rate once safe.

rows.label: Death rate of IRAP's clients while they wait for a pathway (deaths per person-year)
rows.explainer: IRAP's clients are refugees in first countries of asylum and people at risk where they are: US-affiliated Afghans under the Taliban, LGBTQIA+ refugees and women at risk of honour killings in Jordan and Lebanon, Syrians who fear forced return, families in Central America. Anchors: Sudan's crude death rate of 0.0063 a year (@sudan.crude_death_rate_2024): Sudanese refugees are among IRAP's Jordan clients, and Sudan's young population is like the clients'; adult death rates in such places of 3 to 5 per 1,000; and the targeted threats that make many of them IRAP clients. Our judgment 0.007, from 0.004 to 0.015. Read by both IRAP models.

rows.label: Years a client would otherwise have stayed in danger
rows.explainer: How long the acute excess lasts for someone who doesn't get out: protracted refugee situations last a decade or more, but the targeted risk (reprisals, forced return, violence) is highest in the first years and some clients would find another way out; 3 years, from 1 to 5. The long-run health gain of living in a rich country beyond that is in the unmodelled share. Read by both IRAP models.
